papers.conclusion: CaseEdit establishes that a multistage inference-based data generation pipeline offers a promising avenue for modeling human-like commonsense reasoning, and effective editing techniques like AlphaEdit allow small models to internalize context-sensitive knowledge, paving the way for lightweight, personalized assistants.
papers.key_findings:
AlphaEdit outperforms other knowledge editing methods (ROME, MEND, MEMIT, MEMIT-CSK) on the CaseEdit dataset across all evaluated metrics: Reliability, Generalization, Locality, and Portability.
Models exhibit increased uncertainty (decreased confidence in the edited fact) as the number of sequential, unrelated edits scales, but AlphaEdit mitigates this effect due to its null-space projection constraint.
The CaseEdit dataset, built via a multi-stage inference pipeline on ATOMIC 2020, provides a framework for evaluating personalized commonsense knowledge editing in small LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Systematic evaluation was limited by the lack of large-scale human evaluations to assess edit plausibility.
Compute and time constraints restricted the number of edits studied, limiting insights into the scalability of knowledge editing techniques.
The study did not compare knowledge editing techniques with alternative methods like Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) or fine-tuning on the same dataset.
future_direction: Incorporate crowd-sourced evaluations (e.g., via Amazon Mechanical Turk) and an RLHF pipeline to refine edits and improve model alignment.
Compare knowledge editing techniques with alternative approaches like RAG and fine-tuning on the same dataset to highlight respective advantages and limitations.
Investigate the impact of model size on knowledge editing performance and evaluate editing on LLMs specifically trained for reasoning (e.g., DeepSeek-r1).
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong performance on factual recall and general reasoning but struggle to adapt to user-specific, commonsense knowledge, a challenge particularly acute in small-parameter settings where computational efficiency is prioritized. We introduce CaseEdit, a new dataset and generation pipeline for evaluating localized, personalized commonsense knowledge editing in small LLMs to address this. Built upon the ATOMIC20/20 commonsense graph, CaseEdit uses a multi-stage inference process to generate both typical and atypical contextual edits for household objects, paired with targeted evaluation questions across four axes: reliability, generalization, locality, and portability. We evaluate established knowledge editing methods using CaseEdit and demonstrate that AlphaEdit, a technique employing null-space projection to minimize interference with unrelated knowledge, consistently outperforms other methods when applied to an LLaMA 3.2 3B model, even in scalability tests, showing minimal ripple effects. Our results indicate that using CaseEdit with effective editing techniques like AlphaEdit allows small models to internalize high-quality, context-sensitive common-sense knowledge, paving the way for lightweight, personalized assistants.

papers.title: LLM Knowledge is Brittle: Truthfulness Representations Rely on Superficial Resemblance
papers.research_question: Do LLMs learn robust underlying knowledge representations, or are they fragile and tied to the exact phrasings and formulations seen during training?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs' internal representations of statement truthfulness are brittle and degrade under superficial, semantically-preserving transformations, indicating that knowledge representations rely on superficial resemblance to pre-training data rather than robust, generalizable knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LLMs learn shallow, non-robust knowledge representations that fail to generalize to scenarios unlike those seen during training, presenting a fundamental challenge for the utility of truthfulness probes and the reliability of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness separability degrades as samples become more out-of-distribution (OOD) across all probing methods, datasets, and model families.
Certain topics (e.g., sociology, marketing) have more robust representations than others (e.g., history).
Benchmark performance does not imply robust representations; knowledge representations degrade even for questions the model answers correctly.
Larger models may not be more robust; the 70B Llama model showed the steepest degradation in some cases.
The type of transformation affects degradation differently; translation breaks representations while negation does not affect internal probe performance.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to decoder-only autoregressive language models.
Use of perplexity as a proxy for out-of-distribution (OOD) may not be perfect.
Only semantically-preserving transformations are considered.
future_direction: Improving the robustness of learned knowledge representations.
Extending the analysis to other model architectures (e.g., encoder-decoder models).
Exploring other types of distribution shifts beyond superficial transformations.
papers.abstract: For Large Language Models (LLMs) to be reliable, they must learn robust knowledge that can be generally applied in diverse settings -- often unlike those seen during training. Yet, extensive research has shown that LLM performance can be brittle, with models exhibiting excessive sensitivity to trivial input variations. In this work, we explore whether this brittleness is a direct result of unstable internal knowledge representations. To explore this question, we build on previous work showing that LLM representations encode statement truthfulness -- i.e., true, factual statements can be easily separated from false, inaccurate ones. Specifically, we test the robustness of learned knowledge by evaluating representation separability on samples that have undergone superficial transformations to drive them out-of-distribution (OOD), such as typos or reformulations. By applying semantically-preserving perturbations, we study how separability degrades as statements become more OOD, across four LLM families, five evaluation datasets, and three knowledge probing methods. Our results reveal that internal representations of statement truthfulness collapse as the samples' presentations become less similar to those seen during pre-training. While LLMs can often distinguish between true and false statements when they closely resemble the pre-training data, this ability is highly dependent on the statement's exact surface form. These findings offer a possible explanation for brittle benchmark performance: LLMs may learn shallow, non-robust knowledge representations that allow for only limited generalizability. Our work presents a fundamental challenge for the utility of truthfulness probes, and more broadly, calls for further research on improving the robustness of learned knowledge representations.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: Journey to the Center of the Knowledge Neurons: Discoveries of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons and Degenerate Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in multilingual pre-trained language models? Specifically, are there language-independent knowledge neurons and degenerate knowledge neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients (AMIG) method for precise knowledge neuron localization and discovers two novel types of neurons: language-independent knowledge neurons, which store knowledge across languages, and degenerate knowledge neurons, which provide functional overlap for robust fact storage and can be used for fact-checking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that their AMIG method enables precise knowledge localization and reveals two types of neurons that provide insights into knowledge storage, with language-independent neurons enabling cross-lingual editing and degenerate neurons enabling fact-checking.
papers.key_findings:
AMIG localizes knowledge neurons more precisely than previous methods, especially for Chinese datasets.
Knowledge neurons in m-BERT are primarily in the final layers, while in m-GPT they are distributed across early, middle, and final layers.
Language-independent knowledge neurons are concentrated in the final one or two layers and facilitate cross-lingual knowledge editing.
Degenerate knowledge neurons exist and can help PLMs detect wrong facts, improving fact-checking performance.
The existence of degenerate knowledge neurons is not dependent on multilingualism, as they are also found in monolingual models like BERT and GPT-2.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) contain vast amounts of factual knowledge, but how the knowledge is stored in the parameters remains unclear. This paper delves into the complex task of understanding how factual knowledge is stored in multilingual PLMs, and introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients method, which successfully localizes knowledge neurons more precisely compared to current methods, and is more universal across various architectures and languages. Moreover, we conduct an in-depth exploration of knowledge neurons, leading to the following two important discoveries: (1) The discovery of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons, which store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language. We design cross-lingual knowledge editing experiments, demonstrating that the PLMs can accomplish this task based on language-independent neurons; (2) The discovery of Degenerate Knowledge Neurons, a novel type of neuron showing that different knowledge neurons can store the same fact. Its property of functional overlap endows the PLMs with a robust mastery of factual knowledge. We design fact-checking experiments, proving that the degenerate knowledge neurons can help the PLMs to detect wrong facts. Experiments corroborate these findings, shedding light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage in multilingual PLMs, and contribute valuable insights to the field. The code is available at https://github.com/heng840/AMIG.

papers.title: Everything is Editable: Extend Knowledge Editing to Unstructured Data in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to extend knowledge editing to unstructured data in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes UnKE, a method for editing unstructured knowledge in LLMs using non-local block key-value storage and cause-driven optimization.
papers.conclusion: UnKE effectively edits unstructured knowledge in LLMs and surpasses strong baselines.
papers.key_findings:
UnKE outperforms existing baselines on unstructured knowledge editing benchmark UnKEBench.
UnKE demonstrates robust batch editing and sequential editing capabilities.
Knowledge in LLMs is stored non-locally, contradicting the local storage hypothesis.
Term-driven optimization is not robust for unstructured knowledge editing.
UnKE also performs well on structured knowledge editing benchmarks.
papers.limitation: Potential misuse by malicious actors to inject harmful information into LLMs
papers.abstract: Recent knowledge editing methods have primarily focused on modifying structured knowledge in large language models. However, this task setting overlooks the fact that a significant portion of real-world knowledge is stored in an unstructured format, characterized by long-form content, noise, and a complex yet comprehensive nature. Techniques like "local layer key-value storage" and "term-driven optimization", as used in previous methods like MEMIT, are not effective for handling unstructured knowledge. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Unstructured Knowledge Editing method, namely UnKE, which extends previous assumptions in the layer dimension and token dimension. Firstly, in the layer dimension, we propose non-local block key-value storage to replace local layer key-value storage, increasing the representation ability of key-value pairs and incorporating attention layer knowledge. Secondly, in the token dimension, we replace "term-driven optimization" with "cause-driven optimization", which edits the last token directly while preserving context, avoiding the need to locate terms and preventing the loss of context information. Results on newly proposed unstructured knowledge editing dataset (UnKEBench) and traditional structured datasets demonstrate that UnKE achieves remarkable performance, surpassing strong baselines. In addition, UnKE has robust batch editing and sequential editing capabilities.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Dissecting Recall of Factual Associations in Auto-Regressive Language Models
papers.research_question: How do auto-regressive language models internally retrieve factual associations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-step internal mechanism for factual attribute extraction in auto-regressive LMs, involving subject enrichment by early MLPs, relation propagation, and attribute extraction by attention heads.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations are stored in lower layers and extracted by MLP sublayers to form attribute-rich subject representations; upon a query, the attribute is extracted by MHSA sublayers whose parameters often encode subject-attribute mappings.
papers.key_findings:
Critical information flows from relation and then subject positions to the prediction via specific attention edges.
Subject representations are enriched with multiple attributes by early MLP sublayers.
Attribute extraction is primarily performed by upper MHSA sublayers via attention heads that encode subject-attribute mappings.
The extraction mechanism is a three-step process: subject enrichment, relation propagation, and attribute extraction.
Approximately 70% of predictions use this extraction mechanism.
papers.limitation:
Projections to vocabulary space are an approximation, especially in early layers.
Attention knockout may have information leakage across positions, though blocking a range of layers alleviates this.
future_direction: knowledge localization
model editing
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) are known to capture factual knowledge in their parameters. While previous work looked into where factual associations are stored, only little is known about how they are retrieved internally during inference. We investigate this question through the lens of information flow. Given a subject-relation query, we study how the model aggregates information about the subject and relation to predict the correct attribute. With interventions on attention edges, we first identify two critical points where information propagates to the prediction: one from the relation positions followed by another from the subject positions. Next, by analyzing the information at these points, we unveil a three-step internal mechanism for attribute extraction. First, the representation at the last-subject position goes through an enrichment process, driven by the early MLP sublayers, to encode many subject-related attributes. Second, information from the relation propagates to the prediction. Third, the prediction representation "queries" the enriched subject to extract the attribute. Perhaps surprisingly, this extraction is typically done via attention heads, which often encode subject-attribute mappings in their parameters. Overall, our findings introduce a comprehensive view of how factual associations are stored and extracted internally in LMs, facilitating future research on knowledge localization and editing.

papers.title: LLMs Know More Than They Show: On the Intrinsic Representation of LLM Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How much information about truthfulness is encoded in LLMs' internal representations, and how can it be used for error detection and analysis?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode truthfulness information in exact answer tokens, enabling improved error detection and analysis of error types, and revealing that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific rather than universal.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of LLMs encode rich information about truthfulness and error types, which can guide error analysis and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness information is concentrated in exact answer tokens, and leveraging this improves error detection performance.
Error detectors based on probing do not generalize across tasks, indicating that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific.
Internal representations can predict error types (e.g., consistently incorrect, many answers).
There is a discrepancy between internal encoding and external behavior: the model may encode the correct answer but generate an incorrect one.
papers.limitation:
Error detectors do not generalize across datasets.
The error taxonomy is non-orthogonal, with overlapping categories.
future_direction: Further investigation is required to disentangle the multiple mechanisms of truthfulness encoding.
Potential directions for improvements in error analysis and mitigation using the model-centric framework.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce errors, including factual inaccuracies, biases, and reasoning failures, collectively referred to as "hallucinations". Recent studies have demonstrated that LLMs' internal states encode information regarding the truthfulness of their outputs, and that this information can be utilized to detect errors. In this work, we show that the internal representations of LLMs encode much more information about truthfulness than previously recognized. We first discover that the truthfulness information is concentrated in specific tokens, and leveraging this property significantly enhances error detection performance. Yet, we show that such error detectors fail to generalize across datasets, implying that -- contrary to prior claims -- truthfulness encoding is not universal but rather multifaceted. Next, we show that internal representations can also be used for predicting the types of errors the model is likely to make, facilitating the development of tailored mitigation strategies. Lastly, we reveal a discrepancy between LLMs' internal encoding and external behavior: they may encode the correct answer, yet consistently generate an incorrect one. Taken together, these insights deepen our understanding of LLM errors from the model's internal perspective, which can guide future research on enhancing error analysis and mitigation.

papers.title: AlphaEdit: Null-Space Constrained Knowledge Editing for Language Models
papers.research_question: How to update knowledge in large language models without disrupting preserved knowledge, especially in sequential editing scenarios?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AlphaEdit, a knowledge editing method that projects parameter perturbations onto the null space of preserved knowledge to avoid disrupting it during updates.
papers.conclusion: AlphaEdit is an effective and efficient method for knowledge editing that successfully updates target knowledge while preserving existing knowledge and maintaining model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
AlphaEdit improves the performance of existing locating-then-editing methods by an average of 36.7%.
AlphaEdit maintains the general capabilities of post-edited LLMs and prevents degradation in sequential editing.
AlphaEdit prevents overfitting and avoids distributional shifts in hidden representations.
AlphaEdit can be integrated into existing editing methods with a single line of code for projection, significantly boosting their performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit hallucinations due to incorrect or outdated knowledge. Hence, model editing methods have emerged to enable targeted knowledge updates. To achieve this, a prevailing paradigm is the locating-then-editing approach, which first locates influential parameters and then edits them by introducing a perturbation. While effective, current studies have demonstrated that this perturbation inevitably disrupt the originally preserved knowledge within LLMs, especially in sequential editing scenarios. To address this, we introduce AlphaEdit, a novel solution that projects perturbation onto the null space of the preserved knowledge before applying it to the parameters. We theoretically prove that this projection ensures the output of post-edited LLMs remains unchanged when queried about the preserved knowledge, thereby mitigating the issue of disruption. Extensive experiments on various LLMs, including LLaMA3, GPT2-XL, and GPT-J, show that AlphaEdit boosts the performance of most locating-then-editing methods by an average of 36.7% with a single line of additional code for projection solely. Our code is available at: https://github.com/jianghoucheng/AlphaEdit.

papers.title: On the Superimposed Noise Accumulation Problem in Sequential Knowledge Editing of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What causes the decline in editing success rates during sequential knowledge editing of large language models, and how can this be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies the superimposed noise accumulation problem in sequential knowledge editing and proposes DeltaEdit, a method that uses dynamic orthogonal constraints to reduce interference between edits, improving editing performance.
papers.conclusion: DeltaEdit effectively mitigates superimposed noise in sequential knowledge editing, leading to superior editing performance and better preservation of model capabilities and representation integrity.
papers.key_findings:
As the number of sequential edits increases, the model's output deviates from the desired target due to accumulated superimposed noise, leading to a decline in editing success rates.
Superimposed noise is caused by the incorrect activation of irrelevant knowledge and the overlap of influence vectors between edits.
DeltaEdit, which incorporates a dynamic orthogonal constraint strategy to optimize influence vectors, significantly reduces superimposed noise and achieves a 16.8% improvement in editing performance over the strongest baseline.
DeltaEdit better preserves the original distribution of the model's hidden representations compared to other editing methods, helping maintain general capabilities.
The method is particularly effective in scenarios with high object similarity (e.g., CounterFact dataset) and for noise-sensitive models like Llama3-8B.
papers.abstract: Sequential knowledge editing techniques aim to continuously update knowledge in large language models at low cost, preventing models from generating outdated or incorrect information. However, existing sequential editing methods suffer from a significant decline in editing success rates after long-term editing. Through theoretical analysis and experiments, our findings reveal that as the number of edits increases, the model's output increasingly deviates from the desired target, leading to a drop in editing success rates. We refer to this issue as the superimposed noise accumulation problem. Our further analysis demonstrates that the problem is related to the erroneous activation of irrelevant knowledge and conflicts between activated knowledge. Based on this analysis, a method named DeltaEdit is proposed that reduces conflicts between knowledge through dynamic orthogonal constraint strategies. Experiments show that DeltaEdit significantly reduces superimposed noise, achieving a 16.8% improvement in editing performance over the strongest baseline.

papers.title: Model Editing Harms General Abilities of Large Language Models: Regularization to the Rescue
papers.research_question: Does model editing hurt the general abilities of large language models, and how can this be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Model editing significantly degrades the general abilities of LLMs due to overfitting, and a regularization method (RECT) is proposed to mitigate these side effects while preserving editing performance.
papers.conclusion: Model editing unintentionally hurts the general abilities of LLMs, and the proposed RECT regularization method effectively prevents overfitting to editing facts, helping to preserve both editing and general downstream task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Current model editing methods (KN, MEND, ROME, MEMIT) cause significant performance degradation on a wide range of downstream tasks (reasoning, QA, NLI, etc.) even with a single edit.
The side effects are caused by excessive changes to original model weights, leading to overfitting to the edited facts.
The proposed RECT regularization method, which keeps only the top-k% of weight changes with the largest relative change, can mitigate side effects while maintaining over 94% editing performance.
LLMs are not robust to weight perturbations; editing even a small fraction of parameters (less than 1%) can drastically hurt general abilities.
The accumulation of overfitting across sequential edits amplifies the negative impact on general abilities.
papers.limitation: The study of side effects is based on the ZsRE editing dataset, while more complex and diverse side effects may exist on other editing datasets.
future_direction: Explore side effects on more editing datasets.
Investigate whether the mitigation method works for larger numbers of edits and for all tasks.
papers.abstract: Model editing is a technique that edits the large language models (LLMs) with updated knowledge to alleviate hallucinations without resource-intensive retraining. While current model editing methods can effectively modify a model's behavior within a specific area of interest, they often overlook the potential unintended side effects on the general abilities of LLMs such as reasoning, natural language inference, and question answering. In this paper, we raise concerns that model editing's improvements on factuality may come at the cost of a significant degradation of the model's general abilities. We systematically analyze the side effects by evaluating four popular editing methods on three LLMs across eight representative tasks. Our extensive empirical experiments show that it is challenging for current editing methods to simultaneously improve factuality of LLMs and maintain their general abilities. Our analysis reveals that the side effects are caused by model editing altering the original model weights excessively, leading to overfitting to the edited facts. To mitigate this, a method named RECT is proposed to regularize the edit update weights by imposing constraints on their complexity based on the RElative Change in weighT. Evaluation results show that RECT can significantly mitigate the side effects of editing while still maintaining over 94% editing performance.

papers.title: Does Knowledge Localization Hold True? Surprising Differences Between Entity and Relation Perspectives in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether entity and relational knowledge are stored equivalently in language models and where relational knowledge is localized within model parameters.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that entity and relational knowledge are stored separately in language models, with relational knowledge encoded in both MLP and attention layers, challenging previous assumptions that knowledge is primarily localized in MLP weights.
papers.conclusion: This paper reveals that relational knowledge in LLMs is encoded not only in MLP layers but also significantly in attention modules, highlighting the complexity of knowledge storage mechanisms and providing a new foundation for future research in model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Editing entity knowledge does not equivalently edit relational knowledge, and vice versa, indicating they are not interchangeable.
Relational knowledge is localized in both MLP and attention layers, unlike entity knowledge which prior work suggested is primarily in MLP layers.
Knowledge storage location identified through causal tracing differs significantly between entity and relation perspectives.
Model editing from entity and relation perspectives yields inconsistent outcomes, questioning the validity of previous knowledge localization methods.
Factual knowledge is not stored as a single unit; relations and entities are represented separately within model parameters.
papers.abstract: Large language models encapsulate knowledge and have demonstrated superior performance on various natural language processing tasks. Recent studies have localized this knowledge to specific model parameters, such as the MLP weights in intermediate layers. This study investigates the differences between entity and relational knowledge through knowledge editing. Our findings reveal that entity and relational knowledge cannot be directly transferred or mapped to each other. This result is unexpected, as logically, modifying the entity or the relation within the same knowledge triplet should yield equivalent outcomes. To further elucidate the differences between entity and relational knowledge, we employ causal analysis to investigate how relational knowledge is stored in pre-trained models. Contrary to prior research suggesting that knowledge is stored in MLP weights, our experiments demonstrate that relational knowledge is also significantly encoded in attention modules. This insight highlights the multifaceted nature of knowledge storage in language models, underscoring the complexity of manipulating specific types of knowledge within these models.

papers.title: Indications of Belief-Guided Agency and Meta-Cognitive Monitoring in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the behavior of large language models indicate belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring as defined by the HOT-3 indicator for consciousness?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework and the Belief Dominance metric to test the HOT-3 indicator in LLMs, providing empirical evidence for belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the existence of agency guided by a general belief formation and action selection system regulated by meta-cognitive monitoring in LLMs, contributing to the study of AI consciousness.
papers.key_findings:
External manipulations systematically modulate internal belief formation.
Belief formation causally drives the model's action selection.
Models can monitor and report their own belief states, indicating meta-cognitive monitoring.
papers.limitation:
The mechanistic implementation of belief formation, action selection, and meta-cognition remains unclear.
The framework is restricted to capturing beliefs that can be expressed in words.
The framework currently only tests two competing beliefs.
future_direction: Studying the mechanistic implementation of belief formation and meta-cognitive monitoring.
Extending the framework to capture latent beliefs beyond existing vocabulary.
Testing additional consciousness criteria in more capable models.
papers.abstract: Rapid advancements in large language models (LLMs) have sparked the question whether these models possess some form of consciousness. To tackle this challenge, Butlin et al. (2023) introduced a list of indicators for consciousness in artificial systems based on neuroscientific theories. In this work, we evaluate a key indicator from this list, called HOT-3, which tests for agency guided by a general belief-formation and action selection system that updates beliefs based on meta-cognitive monitoring. We view beliefs as representations in the model's latent space that emerge in response to a given input, and introduce a metric to quantify their dominance during generation. Analyzing the dynamics between competing beliefs across models and tasks reveals three key findings: (1) external manipulations systematically modulate internal belief formation, (2) belief formation causally drives the model's action selection, and (3) models can monitor and report their own belief states. Together, these results provide empirical support for the existence of belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring in LLMs. More broadly, our work lays methodological groundwork for investigating the emergence of agency, beliefs, and meta-cognition in LLMs.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Knowledge Localization: Mission Not Accomplished? Enter Query Localization!
papers.research_question: Does the Knowledge Localization (KL) assumption hold for all facts? If not, what is a more realistic assumption?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Query Localization (QL) assumption, which includes query-KN mapping and dynamic KN selection, and introduces a Consistency-Aware KN modification method that improves knowledge editing performance.
papers.conclusion: The Query Localization assumption provides a more realistic framework for understanding knowledge storage and expression in LLMs than the Knowledge Localization assumption, and is validated by improved editing performance.
papers.key_findings:
Inconsistent Knowledge (KI) that violates the Knowledge Localization assumption is widespread in LLMs.
For KI, knowledge neurons are associated with specific queries rather than the fact itself (query-KN mapping).
The attention module plays a key role in selecting appropriate knowledge neurons for expression (dynamic KN selection).
The proposed Consistency-Aware KN modification method, based on the QL assumption, improves knowledge editing performance over baseline methods.
papers.limitation:
The work primarily focuses on factual knowledge, and it remains unclear whether the QL assumption applies to other types of knowledge.
The distinction between Consistent Knowledge (KC) and Inconsistent Knowledge (KI) might be related to the pre-training process.
future_direction: Exploring how to reconcile the QL assumption with other current theories.
Further utilizing the QL assumption to improve model editing methods.
Integrating the attention module more effectively to develop enhanced methods for dynamically editing knowledge.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) store extensive factual knowledge, but the mechanisms behind how they store and express this knowledge remain unclear. The Knowledge Neuron (KN) thesis is a prominent theory for explaining these mechanisms. This theory is based on the Knowledge Localization (KL) assumption, which suggests that a fact can be localized to a few knowledge storage units, namely knowledge neurons. However, this assumption has two limitations: first, it may be too rigid regarding knowledge storage, and second, it neglects the role of the attention module in knowledge expression. In this paper, we first re-examine the KL assumption and demonstrate that its limitations do indeed exist. To address these, we then present two new findings, each targeting one of the limitations: one focusing on knowledge storage and the other on knowledge expression. We summarize these findings as \textbf{Query Localization} (QL) assumption and argue that the KL assumption can be viewed as a simplification of the QL assumption. Based on QL assumption, we further propose the Consistency-Aware KN modification method, which improves the performance of knowledge modification, further validating our new assumption. We conduct 39 sets of experiments, along with additional visualization experiments, to rigorously confirm our conclusions. Code is available at https://github.com/heng840/KnowledgeLocalization.

papers.title: Representation in large language models
papers.research_question: Is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, contrary to the look-up table view, and outlines how mechanistic interpretability methods can be used to study these representations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do use representation-based information processing, and we can investigate these representations using mechanistic interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
The look-up table view of LLMs is inadequate because it cannot explain robust behavior.
Representations, as defined by four conditions (INFORMATION, EXPLOITABILITY, BEHAVIOR, ROLE), can explain robust behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability methods like probing and causal interventions can test for representations in LLMs.
papers.abstract: The extraordinary success of recent Large Language Models (LLMs) on a diverse array of tasks has led to an explosion of scientific and philosophical theorizing aimed at explaining how they do what they do. Unfortunately, disagreement over fundamental theoretical issues has led to stalemate, with entrenched camps of LLM optimists and pessimists often committed to very different views of how these systems work. Overcoming stalemate requires agreement on fundamental questions, and the goal of this paper is to address one such question, namely: is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up? This is a question about what kind of algorithm LLMs implement, and the answer carries serious implications for higher level questions about whether these systems have beliefs, intentions, concepts, knowledge, and understanding. I argue that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, and then I describe and defend a series of practical techniques for investigating these representations and developing explanations on their basis. The resulting account provides a groundwork for future theorizing about language models and their successors.

papers.title: Tracing Facts or just Copies? A critical investigation of the Competitions of Mechanisms in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in LLMs mediate the competition between factual recall from parametric memory and counterfactual information provided in context? Do they perform selective counterfactual suppression or general copy suppression, and are they domain-specific?
papers.core_contribution: Attention heads that promote factual output in LLMs operate via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, and their behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models showing more specialization.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that attention heads mediate the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens via copy suppression, and their effects are domain-dependent, with implications for model interpretability and control.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads contribute to the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens, and modifying their strength affects the proportion of factual outputs.
The attention heads supporting factual tokens suppress copying in general, not just counterfactuals, as they also suppress factual tokens when facts are present in the prompt.
The effect of attention heads is sensitive to sentence structure and the presence of hints (factual token in the subject).
Attention heads exhibit domain specialization; their contribution varies by answer category (e.g., location, language, organization).
Larger models (Pythia-6.9B) show more specialized and category-sensitive patterns than smaller models (GPT-2).
papers.limitation: The experiments are limited to two models (GPT-2 and Pythia-6.9B) and do not cover more models or study attention modification of different heads on different domains in detail.
future_direction: Applying the methods to different models
Studying how each attention head interacts with different domains
Constructing new datasets on other domains (e.g., STEM) and applying similar techniques
papers.abstract: This paper presents a reproducibility study examining how Large Language Models (LLMs) manage competing factual and counterfactual information, focusing on the role of attention heads in this process. We attempt to reproduce and reconcile findings from three recent studies by Ortu et al., Yu, Merullo, and Pavlick and McDougall et al. that investigate the competition between model-learned facts and contradictory context information through Mechanistic Interpretability tools. Our study specifically examines the relationship between attention head strength and factual output ratios, evaluates competing hypotheses about attention heads' suppression mechanisms, and investigates the domain specificity of these attention patterns. Our findings suggest that attention heads promoting factual output do so via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, as strengthening them can also inhibit correct facts. Additionally, we show that attention head behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models exhibiting more specialized and category-sensitive patterns.

papers.title: Assessing Knowledge Editing in Language Models via Relation Perspective
papers.research_question: Whether existing entity-centric knowledge editing methods are suitable for relation-centric editing, and where relation knowledge is stored in transformers.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a new benchmark for relation-based knowledge editing (RaKE) and shows that existing editing methods underperform on relation editing because they only modify the FFN, while relation knowledge is also stored in attention layers.
papers.conclusion: Current editing methods are insufficient for relation-based editing because they focus only on the FFN and ignore the attention layer, which also stores relation knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods perform significantly worse on relation-based editing compared to entity-based editing.
Relation knowledge is stored not only in the feed-forward network (FFN) but also in the attention layers of transformers.
papers.limitation:
The RaKE dataset lacks an assessment of relation specificity performance.
There is a lack of specific methods for editing relations.
future_direction: Explore the correlation and differences between entity and relation knowledge in language models.
Develop relation-based editing methods that also modify the attention module.
papers.abstract: Knowledge Editing (KE) for modifying factual knowledge in Large Language Models (LLMs) has been receiving increasing attention. However, existing knowledge editing methods are entity-centric, and it is unclear whether this approach is suitable for a relation-centric perspective. To address this gap, this paper constructs a new benchmark named RaKE, which focuses on Relation based Knowledge Editing. In this paper, we establish a suite of innovative metrics for evaluation and conduct comprehensive experiments involving various knowledge editing baselines. We notice that existing knowledge editing methods exhibit the potential difficulty in their ability to edit relations. Therefore, we further explore the role of relations in factual triplets within the transformer. Our research results confirm that knowledge related to relations is not only stored in the FFN network but also in the attention layers. This provides experimental support for future relation-based knowledge editing methods.

papers.title: EVEDIT: Event-based Knowledge Editing for Deterministic Knowledge Propagation
papers.research_question: How can knowledge editing in large language models be improved to reduce uncertainty and enable confident knowledge propagation by addressing the issue of undefined deduction anchors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces event-based knowledge editing to reduce uncertainty in knowledge propagation, proposes the EVEDIT benchmark, and presents the Self-Edit method which improves consistency while maintaining naturalness.
papers.conclusion: Event-based knowledge editing provides a more robust and practical setting for knowledge editing, and the Self-Edit method effectively improves consistency while preserving naturalness.
papers.key_findings:
Current triple-based knowledge editing leads to uncertainty in models due to undefined deduction anchors.
Event-based editing reduces uncertainty and improves model confidence.
The proposed Self-Edit method achieves significant improvement in factual consistency while maintaining naturalness.
Factual-association editing methods fail on event-based editing and harm naturalness.
In-context learning approaches (including RAG) perform well but have scalability limitations.
papers.limitation: There is still a significant gap toward a satisfying characterization of editing boundaries in edited models.
future_direction: Adding extra instruction-tuning data to improve performance further.
Developing better RAG-based methods for event-based knowledge editing.
Exploring the use of structured knowledge such as knowledge graphs to guide LLMs in knowledge editing.

papers.title: Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that knowledge-conflicting facts are most enduring in language models and proposes a sparsification method to erase them while preserving task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper discovers that knowledge-conflicting facts endure for many updates and cause inappropriate priming, and shows that their impact can be mitigated via multi-step sparse updates while preserving main task training.
papers.key_findings:
Facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while mundane and scrambled facts are forgotten more rapidly.
Knowledge-conflicting facts can prime how the model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts.
There is a sweet spot in fact novelty (between consistency and randomness) for memory durability.
The impact of knowledge-conflicting facts can be erased by multi-step sparse updates while preserving task performance.
future_direction: Extend the Outlandish dataset further
papers.abstract: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train? We investigate this question by injecting facts into LMs from a new probing dataset, "Outlandish", which is designed to permit the testing of a spectrum of different fact types. When studying how robust these memories are, there appears to be a sweet spot in the spectrum of fact novelty between consistency with world knowledge and total randomness, where the injected memory is the most enduring. Specifically we show that facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while prompts not conflicting with common knowledge (mundane), as well as scrambled prompts (randomly jumbled) are both forgotten much more rapidly. Further, knowledge-conflicting facts can "prime'' how the language model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts, showing their propensity for non-target generalization, while both mundane and randomly jumbled facts prime significantly less. Finally, we show that impacts of knowledge-conflicting facts in LMs, though they can be long lasting, can be largely erased by novel application of multi-step sparse updates, even while the training ability of the model is preserved. As such, this very simple procedure has direct implications for mitigating the effects of data poisoning in training.

papers.title: ChainEdit: Propagating Ripple Effects in LLM Knowledge Editing through Logical Rule-Guided Chains
papers.research_question: How to maintain logical consistency when propagating ripple effects to associated facts during knowledge editing in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ChainEdit, a framework that synergizes knowledge graph-derived logical rules with LLMs' logical reasoning to enable systematic chain updates during knowledge editing, improving logical generalization.
papers.conclusion: ChainEdit effectively addresses the ripple effect in knowledge editing by using logical rules to propagate edits, establishing new state-of-the-art performance on logical generalization while ensuring internal logical consistency.
papers.key_findings:
ChainEdit improves logical generalization by over 30% on the RIPPLE EDITS benchmark while maintaining editing reliability and specificity.
The framework is compatible with various editing methods (MEMIT, LoRA, FT) and works across different model sizes.
Rule alignment with LLMs' internal logic is crucial for performance, outperforming pure KG-based rule mining.
Proposed dataset variants (filtered, replaced, in-prompt) address evaluation biases in existing benchmarks.
ChainEdit demonstrates robust performance even when intermediate knowledge is provided in context or replaced with model-generated content.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on knowledge graphs for rule mining, which may have limited coverage and cannot capture all logical relationships.
The reasoning capability of LLMs, especially smaller models, may limit accurate understanding and application of complex rules.
Current rule mining strategy retains only universally applicable rules, overlooking conditionally valid rules.
As the rule set expands, the number of edits may grow exponentially, potentially affecting system performance.
future_direction: Introduce conditional rule and selective application to handle rules valid only under specific conditions.
Introduce optimization strategies such as rule priority mechanisms or rule application conditions to manage scalability.
papers.abstract: Current knowledge editing methods for large language models (LLMs) struggle to maintain logical consistency when propagating ripple effects to associated facts.We propose ChainEdit, a framework that synergizes knowledge graph-derived logical rules with LLM logical reasoning capabilities to enable systematic chain updates.By automatically extracting logical patterns from structured knowledge bases and aligning them with LLMs' internal logics, ChainEdit dynamically generates and edits logically connected knowledge clusters.Experiments demonstrate an improvement of more than 30% in logical generalization over baselines while preserving editing reliability and specificity.We further address evaluation biases in existing benchmarks through knowledge-aware protocols that disentangle external dependencies.This work establishes new state-of-the-art performance on ripple effect while ensuring internal logical consistency after knowledge editing.

papers.title: Knowledge Editing in Language Models via Adapted Direct Preference Optimization
papers.research_question: How can knowledge editing in large language models be effectively performed by adapting direct preference optimization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Knowledge Direct Preference Optimization (KDPO), a variant of DPO optimized for knowledge editing, which shows improved performance in sequential edits and better locality compared to existing methods.
papers.conclusion: KDPO is a high-performance and precise method for knowledge editing in LLMs, which can significantly help prevent expensive retraining due to factual errors.
papers.key_findings:
KDPO outperforms baseline knowledge editing methods on multiple datasets and models, especially in the locality metric.
The method maintains state-of-the-art performance for both 100 and 500 sequential edits.
KDPO preserves the model's general capabilities, as shown by minimal performance degradation on benchmarks like HellaSwag, Winogrande, and MMLU.
The method is effective even on small language models (e.g., Qwen1.5-0.5B).
KDPO demonstrates superior locality and precision compared to vanilla DPO, particularly as the number of sequential edits increases.
papers.limitation: The need to keep a copy of the model (reference model) increases the memory footprint.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can become outdated over time as they may lack updated world knowledge, leading to factual knowledge errors and gaps. Knowledge Editing (KE) aims to overcome this challenge using weight updates that do not require expensive retraining. We propose treating KE as an LLM alignment problem. Toward this goal, we introduce Knowledge Direct Preference Optimization (KDPO), a variation of the Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) that is more effective for knowledge modifications. Our method is based on an online approach that continually updates the knowledge stored in the model. We use the current knowledge as a negative sample and the new knowledge we want to introduce as a positive sample in a process called DPO. We also use teacher-forcing for negative sample generation and optimize using the positive sample, which helps maintain localized changes. We tested our KE method on various datasets and models, comparing it to several cutting-edge methods, with 100 and 500 sequential edits. Additionally, we conducted an ablation study comparing our method to the standard DPO approach. Our experimental results show that our modified DPO method allows for more refined KE, achieving similar or better performance compared to previous methods.

papers.title: Reasoning as State Transition: A Representational Analysis of Reasoning Evolution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does reasoning ability evolve during training in large language models, and what is the role of internal representation dynamics in this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a representational analysis framework showing that post-training yields limited improvement in static initial representation quality, but reasoning involves a continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, which post-training enhances to drive representations toward a better state for task solving.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel representational perspective on reasoning evolution in LLMs, highlighting the importance of internal state dynamics and the role of post-training in enhancing state transitions, offering insights for future model analysis and optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality.
Reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, unlike non-reasoning tasks.
Post-training empowers models to drive this representation transition toward a better distribution for task solving.
There is a high correlation between generation correctness and final representations, but low correlation with initial representations.
The semantic content of the generated tokens is the dominant driver of the state transition, not additional computation or intrinsic parameter differences.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have achieved remarkable performance on reasoning tasks, motivating research into how this ability evolves during training. Prior work has primarily analyzed this evolution via explicit generation outcomes, treating the reasoning process as a black box and obscuring internal changes. To address this opacity, we introduce a representational perspective to investigate the dynamics of the model's internal states. Through comprehensive experiments across models at various training stages, we discover that post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality. Furthermore, we reveal that, distinct from non-reasoning tasks, reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation. Comparative analysis indicates that post-training empowers models to drive this transition toward a better distribution for task solving. To clarify the relationship between internal states and external outputs, statistical analysis confirms a high correlation between generation correctness and the final representations; while counterfactual experiments identify the semantics of the generated tokens, rather than additional computation during inference or intrinsic parameter differences, as the dominant driver of the transition. Collectively, we offer a novel understanding of the reasoning process and the effect of training on reasoning enhancement, providing valuable insights for future model analysis and optimization.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: NeuroFaith: Evaluating LLM Self-Explanation Faithfulness via Internal Representation Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we measure the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations by aligning them with the model's internal reasoning processes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroFaith, a framework that measures faithfulness of LLM self-explanations by extracting concepts from explanations and mechanistically testing their influence on predictions, and shows how to detect and improve faithfulness via linear probing and steering.
papers.conclusion: NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models tend to produce more faithful and correct self-explanations.
Models can arrive at correct answers through alternative reasoning pathways that bypass explicit bridge object computation (shortcut learning).
There is a gap between internal reasoning and expressed explanations, which decreases with model size.
NeuroFaith outperforms existing faithfulness measures (Counterfactual Intervention and Attribution Agreement) in several settings.
Faithfulness can be linearly detected in representation space and improved through steering.
papers.limitation: Human annotation for concept extraction is costly and may not scale, while LLM-as-a-Judge approaches offer scalability but may miss relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate plausible free text self-explanations to justify their answers. However, these natural language explanations may not accurately reflect the model's actual reasoning process, pinpointing a lack of faithfulness. Existing faithfulness evaluation methods rely primarily on behavioral tests or computational block analysis without examining the semantic content of internal neural representations. This paper proposes NeuroFaith, a flexible framework that measures the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanation by identifying key concepts within explanations and mechanistically testing whether these concepts actually influence the model's predictions. We show the versatility of NeuroFaith across 2-hop reasoning and classification tasks. Additionally, we develop a linear faithfulness probe based on NeuroFaith to detect unfaithful self-explanations from representation space and improve faithfulness through steering. NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.

papers.title: Balancing Knowledge Updates: Toward Unified Modular Editing in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can knowledge editing in LLMs be improved by jointly updating both MLP and Attention modules, rather than focusing solely on MLP modules?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces IntAttn-Edit, a novel knowledge editing method that jointly updates both MLP and Attention modules using a knowledge balancing strategy, which proportionally allocates update magnitudes based on each module's measured contribution to knowledge storage.
papers.conclusion: IntAttn-Edit addresses the limitation of knowledge residuals in existing methods by jointly editing MLP and Attention modules, leading to more balanced and comprehensive knowledge updates that outperform existing approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Attention modules play a substantial role in factual knowledge storage and retrieval, especially in earlier layers, functioning as key-value associative memory structures.
IntAttn-Edit consistently outperforms existing editing baselines (e.g., ROME, MEMIT, AlphaEdit) on benchmarks like ZsRE and WikiData counterfact, achieving higher edit success and portability.
The proposed knowledge balancing strategy, which dynamically allocates update magnitudes between MLP and Attn modules based on their causal contributions, maintains editing performance within an optimal range.
Updating only a subset of knowledge-storage modules (e.g., only MLP) can leave residual outdated knowledge, which IntAttn-Edit mitigates by jointly editing both modules.
Extensive experiments show IntAttn-Edit delivers superior results across different batch sizes and models while maintaining high locality and fluency.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing has emerged as an efficient approach for updating factual knowledge in large language models (LLMs). It typically locates knowledge storage modules and then modifies their parameters. However, most existing methods focus on the weights of multilayer perceptron (MLP) modules, which are often identified as the main repositories of factual information. Other components, such as attention (Attn) modules, are often ignored during editing. This imbalance can leave residual outdated knowledge and limit editing effectiveness. We perform comprehensive knowledge localization experiments on advanced LLMs and find that Attn modules play a substantial role in factual knowledge storage and retrieval, especially in earlier layers. Based on these insights, we propose IntAttn-Edit, a method that extends the associative memory paradigm to jointly update both MLP and Attn modules. Our approach uses a knowledge balancing strategy that allocates update magnitudes in proportion to each module's measured contribution to knowledge storage. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that IntAttn-Edit achieves higher edit success, better generalization, and stronger knowledge preservation than prior methods. Further analysis shows that the balancing strategy keeps editing performance within an optimal range across diverse settings.

papers.title: Editing Common Sense in Transformers
papers.research_question: Whether commonsense judgments are causally associated with localized, editable parameters in Transformers, and if so, can model editing effectively repair incorrect commonsense plausibility judgments?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates strong causal relations between commonsense plausibility judgments and early MLP layers in Transformers, and introduces MEMIT_CSK, an improved model editing method for commonsense that outperforms fine-tuning baselines.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that commonsense knowledge is localized in early MLP layers and can be effectively edited with MEMIT_CSK, providing a compelling direction for incorporating commonsense feedback into transformers through direct model editing.
papers.key_findings:
High task performance is crucial for achieving strong causal tracing results.
Targeted part of speech and layer locations affect causal tracing conclusions and edit success.
MEMIT_CSK exhibits configuration generalization (hyperparameters transfer well to unseen data).
MEMIT_CSK exhibits semantic generalization (balances affected and unaffected neighborhoods).
MEMIT_CSK outperforms fine-tuning for repairing commonsense knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Unable to investigate larger open-sourced models like GPT-J and GPT-NeoX due to resource limitations.
Focus on the binary plausibility prediction task, while parameter editing could improve models on various commonsense tasks.
The optimal edit token (subject, verb, or object) varies among datasets; a single generalized optimal edit token requires further investigation.
future_direction: Investigating the research questions on larger models.
Extending parameter editing to improve models on various commonsense tasks.
Further investigation into the existence of a single generalized optimal edit token.
papers.abstract: Editing model parameters directly in Transformers makes updating open-source transformer-based models possible without re-training (Meng et al., 2023). However, these editing methods have only been evaluated on statements about encyclopedic knowledge with a single correct answer. Commonsense knowledge with multiple correct answers, e.g., an apple can be green or red but not transparent, has not been studied but is as essential for enhancing transformers' reliability and usefulness. In this paper, we investigate whether commonsense judgments are causally associated with localized, editable parameters in Transformers, and we provide an affirmative answer. We find that directly applying the MEMIT editing algorithm results in sub-par performance and improve it for the commonsense domain by varying edit tokens and improving the layer selection strategy, i.e., $MEMIT_{CSK}$. GPT-2 Large and XL models edited using $MEMIT_{CSK}$ outperform best-fine-tuned baselines by 10.97% and 10.73% F1 scores on PEP3k and 20Q datasets. In addition, we propose a novel evaluation dataset, PROBE SET, that contains unaffected and affected neighborhoods, affected paraphrases, and affected reasoning challenges. $MEMIT_{CSK}$ performs well across the metrics while fine-tuning baselines show significant trade-offs between unaffected and affected metrics. These results suggest a compelling future direction for incorporating feedback about common sense into Transformers through direct model editing.

papers.title: Investigating Multi-Hop Factual Shortcuts in Knowledge Editing of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the possibilities for LLMs to utilize factual shortcuts based on direct connections between initial and terminal entities in multi-hop knowledge, and what risks do these shortcuts pose in knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates multi-hop factual shortcuts in LLMs, finding that shortcuts correlate with entity co-occurrence frequency in pre-training corpora and contribute to knowledge editing failures, and proposes erasing shortcut neurons to mitigate these risks.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that factual shortcuts compromise the reasoning consistency of LLMs in knowledge editing, and while erasing neurons mitigates risks, fundamental elimination requires changes during pre-training.
papers.key_findings:
Factual shortcuts exist in LLMs for multi-hop knowledge, and their strength is highly correlated with the frequency of co-occurrence of initial and terminal entities in pre-training corpora.
Few-shot prompting leverages more shortcuts in answering multi-hop questions compared to chain-of-thought prompting.
Approximately 20% of failures in multi-hop knowledge editing are attributed to factual shortcuts.
Shortcut failure instances have higher co-occurrence frequencies of initial and terminal entities in the pre-training corpus.
Erasing crucial neurons associated with factual shortcuts reduces the failure rate of multi-hop knowledge editing caused by shortcuts.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is based on the MQUAKE-CF-3K dataset, which may not generalize to other datasets.
Erasing shortcuts is a mitigative measure and cannot completely eliminate them; fundamental elimination requires pre-training changes.
Experiments are limited to GPT-J and LLaMA-2, not covering all publicly accessible LLMs.
future_direction: Extend statistical analyses to more expansive corpora.
Conduct comprehensive experiments on a broader spectrum of LLMs.
Address the elimination of factual shortcuts during the pre-training phase.
papers.abstract: Recent work has showcased the powerful capability of large language models (LLMs) in recalling knowledge and reasoning. However, the reliability of LLMs in combining these two capabilities into reasoning through multi-hop facts has not been widely explored. This paper systematically investigates the possibilities for LLMs to utilize shortcuts based on direct connections between the initial and terminal entities of multi-hop knowledge. We first explore the existence of factual shortcuts through Knowledge Neurons, revealing that: (i) the strength of factual shortcuts is highly correlated with the frequency of co-occurrence of initial and terminal entities in the pre-training corpora; (ii) few-shot prompting leverage more shortcuts in answering multi-hop questions compared to chain-of-thought prompting. Then, we analyze the risks posed by factual shortcuts from the perspective of multi-hop knowledge editing. Analysis shows that approximately 20% of the failures are attributed to shortcuts, and the initial and terminal entities in these failure instances usually have higher co-occurrences in the pre-training corpus.
